Question: Jamar bought some pencils costing more than a penny each at the school bookstore and paid \(\$1.43.\) Sharona bought some of the same pencils and paid \(\$1.87.\) How many more pencils did Sharona buy than Jamar?
Solution:
Using the recorded retail convention that each pencil’s price is a whole number of cents, that price must divide both purchase totals, \(143\) cents and \(187\) cents.

The positive factors of \(143\) are \(1,11,13,143\). Among these, only \(1\) and \(11\) divide \(187\), since \(187=11\cdot17\). The pencils cost more than one cent each, so their price must be \(11\) cents.

Jamar bought \(143\div11=13\) pencils, and Sharona bought \(187\div11=17\). Therefore, Sharona bought \(17-13=\boxed{4}\) more pencils, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
